title: Al-Fatihah
label: Plain-English commentary
intro:
Al-Fatihah is the surah the Qur'an opens with and the surah every prayer opens with. It has seven verses, and the scholars count twenty-five words and one hundred and thirteen letters in it. It was revealed in Makkah, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and Abū al-ʿĀliyah stated. Short as it is, the Prophet ﷺ called it the greatest surah in the Qur'an and said that nothing like it had been sent down in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms or the Qur'an itself.

The surah moves in a single arc. It begins with the name of Allah and His mercy (verse 1), states that all praise belongs to Him as Lord of all worlds (verse 2), names His mercy again and His ownership of the Day of Judgment (verses 3 and 4), turns to Him with the declaration that He alone is worshipped and He alone is asked for help (verse 5), and ends with the request for guidance along the Straight Path, defined by the people who walk it and by the people who have left it (verses 6 and 7). Praise comes first, then the pledge, then the plea.

### What its names mean

- **Al-Fatihah**, the Opener of the Book: the Qur'an starts with it and the prayer is begun with it.
- **Umm al-Kitāb** and **Umm al-Qur'ān**, the Mother of the Book, the name used by most scholars. One explanation is that the Qur'an and the prayer both begin with it. Another is that it contains the meanings of the whole Qur'an. Ibn Jarīr explained that the Arabs call anything comprehensive that holds several particular things within it an umm: the membrane around the brain is umm ar-raʾs, the flag the army gathers around is an umm, and Makkah is Umm al-Qurā, the Mother of Towns, because it is the greatest of them and leads them, and because it was said that the earth was spread out starting from it.
- **As-Sabʿ al-Mathānī**, the seven oft-repeated verses. Abū Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Al-ḥamdu lillāhi Rabbil-ʿālamīn is the Mother of the Qur'an, the Mother of the Book, and the seven repeated verses of the Glorious Qur'an." At-Tirmidhī recorded this and graded it ṣaḥīḥ, and Aḥmad and Ibn Jarīr recorded similar wordings. The Qur'an refers to the surah this way in 15:87, "We have given you the seven oft-repeated verses."
- **Al-Ḥamd**, the Praise, after its opening word.
- **Aṣ-Ṣalāh**, the Prayer, because reciting it is a condition for the prayer to be valid, and because of the hadith in which Allah says, "I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant," and then goes through its verses one by one.
- **Ash-Shifāʾ**, the Cure, and **Ar-Ruqyah**, the Remedy, after the story of the Companion who treated a poisoned chief with it.

### How many verses, and where the basmalah stands

There is no disagreement that the surah has seven verses. Where they differ is over the first line, "In the Name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful": according to most of the reciters of Kūfah, a group of the Companions and their Successors and many later scholars, it is a separate verse at the head of the surah, while others count the seven differently. That question is taken up under verse 1.

### Its virtues

Abū Saʿīd ibn al-Muʿallā said that he was praying when the Prophet ﷺ called him, and he did not answer until he had finished. The Prophet ﷺ asked what had stopped him from coming, reminded him of the verse "Answer Allah and the Messenger when he calls you to what gives you life," and said, "I will teach you the greatest surah in the Qur'an before you leave the mosque." He took him by the hand, and when they were about to leave, Abū Saʿīd reminded him. He said, "Yes: Al-ḥamdu lillāhi Rabbil-ʿālamīn. It is the seven oft-repeated verses and the Glorious Qur'an that I was given." Aḥmad recorded this, and so did al-Bukhārī, Abū Dāwūd, an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb had the same experience. The Prophet ﷺ called him twice while he was praying, and when Ubayy came he asked why he had not answered, reminded him of the same verse, and said, "Would you like me to teach you a surah the like of which has not been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms or the Qur'an?" He kept hold of Ubayy's hand while they walked to the door, and Ubayy walked slowly, afraid they would reach it before he was told. At the door he asked, and the Prophet ﷺ asked him what he recited in the prayer. Ubayy recited the Mother of the Qur'an, and the Prophet ﷺ said, "By Him in whose hand is my soul, Allah has never revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms or the Qur'an a surah like it. It is the seven oft-repeated verses that I was given." Aḥmad recorded it, and at-Tirmidhī recorded it and graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Anas ibn Mālik reported something similar. In the wording of an-Nasāʾī, which at-Tirmidhī graded ḥasan gharīb, the Prophet ﷺ said, "Allah has never revealed in the Torah or the Gospel anything like the Mother of the Qur'an. It is the seven oft-repeated verses, and it is divided into two halves between Allah and His servant."

ʿAbdullāh ibn Jābir said that he greeted the Prophet ﷺ three times after he had poured out water to purify himself and received no answer, followed him home, and sat in the mosque sad and downcast. The Prophet ﷺ came out after his purification, returned his greeting three times with "Peace and the mercy of Allah be upon you," and said, "Shall I tell you the best surah in the Qur'an? Recite 'All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds' to the end." Aḥmad recorded this with a good chain. Some scholars took this hadith as proof that some verses and surahs have more merit than others.

Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī told of a journey on which a servant girl came to say that the chief of her people had been stung or poisoned and their men were away, and asked whether anyone could treat him. A man whose skill none of them had suspected went with her, recited over the chief, and he recovered. The chief gave him thirty sheep and some milk. When he came back his companions asked whether he had known a remedy before, and he said, "I only recited the Mother of the Book over him." They agreed to do nothing with the sheep until they had asked the Prophet ﷺ. When they told him in Madinah, he said, "How did he know that it is a remedy? Divide the sheep, and keep a share for me." Al-Bukhārī recorded it.

Ibn ʿAbbās reported, in a hadith recorded by Muslim and an-Nasāʾī, that while Jibrīl (Gabriel) was with the Prophet ﷺ he heard a sound above him, looked up and said, "This is a door in heaven that has been opened today and has never been opened before." An angel came down through it, came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "Rejoice in two lights you have been given that no prophet before you was given: the Opening of the Book and the closing verses of Sūrat al-Baqarah. You will not recite a letter of them without being given what it holds."

### The surah and the prayer

Abū Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said three times, "Whoever prays a prayer in which he does not recite the Mother of the Qur'an, his prayer is incomplete." Muslim recorded it. When Abū Hurayrah was asked what to do when standing behind the imam, he said, "Recite it to yourself," and then related the hadith in which Allah says, "I have divided the prayer into two halves between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for," answering each verse of the surah in turn. Muslim and an-Nasāʾī also recorded the wording "Half of it is for Me and half for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for." The word "prayer" is used in that hadith for the recitation of the Fatihah. The Qur'an speaks the same way when it says "offer your prayer neither aloud nor in a low voice, but follow a way between," which Ibn ʿAbbās explained, in a report in the Ṣaḥīḥ, as referring to the recitation in the prayer, and when it calls the dawn prayer "the recitation of the Qur'an in the early dawn," the prayer which, as the two Ṣaḥīḥs record, the angels of the night and the angels of the day both attend. The point of the division is that reciting the Qur'an is one of the greatest pillars of the prayer.

From this the scholars drew the ruling, on which there is consensus, that reciting the Fatihah in the prayer is required, by the imam and by those praying behind him, in every prayer and in every unit of it. ʿUbādah ibn aṣ-Ṣāmit reported the Prophet ﷺ saying, "There is no prayer for the one who does not recite the Opening of the Book," recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, and Abū Hurayrah reported, in the Ṣaḥīḥs of Ibn Khuzaymah and Ibn Ḥibbān, "The prayer in which the Mother of the Qur'an is not recited is invalid."

### In short

- Seven verses, revealed in Makkah, recited in every unit of every prayer.
- Its names describe it: the Opener of the Book, the Mother of the Book, the seven oft-repeated verses, the Praise, the Prayer, the Cure.
- The Prophet ﷺ called it the greatest surah in the Qur'an, unlike anything revealed in the earlier scriptures, and one of two lights given to no prophet before him.
- It is a conversation: Allah answers each of its verses as the servant recites it, and the servant is given what he asks for.
- It runs from praise of Allah, through the pledge to worship and rely on Him alone, to the request for guidance.

1.text:
The Qur'an opens with the words "In the Name of Allah—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful". This line, the basmalah, stands at the head of every surah except the ninth, it is the first thing a Muslim says before eating, before setting out, before beginning anything that matters, and it is the first line of the Opening of the Book that is recited in every unit of every prayer. The Companions began the written Qur'an with it. In one short sentence it does three things: it ties the act that follows to Allah, it names Him by the name that belongs to Him alone, and it describes Him by the two names of mercy before any other attribute is mentioned.

The verse is tied to a sentence that comes just before it in practice, the istiʿādhah or seeking of refuge from Shayṭān, which the Qur'an commands before every recitation. The rulings on both, the question of whether the basmalah is a verse of this surah, and the meaning of each of its words are explained below.

### Phrase by phrase

**"In the Name of"** translates bi-smi, which is two words joined: the preposition bi and the noun ism, "name". The preposition has several senses in Arabic, and three of them fit here at the same time: closeness or accompaniment, seeking help, and seeking blessing. So the phrase means "with the name of Allah", "with the help of the name of Allah" and "with the blessing of the name of Allah" all at once. On its own the sentence is incomplete, because the act being done "in the name of Allah" is left unspoken. Arabic grammar supplies a verb that fits the occasion, such as "I begin" or "I recite", and the fitting place for that unspoken verb is after the name, not before it, so that the beginning is made with Allah's name itself and nothing comes ahead of it. The preposition has to stand before the name, because that is how the language works, but even here the written Qur'an makes a small adjustment. In the copy prepared under ʿUthmān with the agreement of the Companions, the alif that would normally be written between the bi and the sīn of ism is dropped, so that the bi is joined straight on to the word "name" and the writing itself begins, in effect, with the name of Allah. In every other place where the same two words meet, as in "Read with the name of your Lord", the alif is kept. The dropping of it belongs to the basmalah alone.

**"Allah"** is the name of the Lord, the proper name of His Essence, the greatest and most comprehensive of His names. It has no plural and no dual, because He is One and has no partner, and no one else can be given it. Some scholars hold that it is the Greatest Name, al-Ism al-Aʿẓam, the name a hadith describes as carrying such blessing that a prayer made with it is granted, though reports differ as to which name that is. One reason for calling it the greatest is that all the other names are used to describe it. In the verses "He is Allah, besides whom there is no god, the Knower of the unseen and the seen, He is the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful. He is Allah, besides whom there is no god, the King, the Holy, the One free from defect, the Giver of security, the Watcher, the Almighty, the Compeller, the Supreme. He is Allah, the Creator, the Maker, the Giver of forms, to Him belong the Best Names" (59:22-24), a whole series of names is attached to "Allah" as its attributes. "The Most Beautiful Names belong to Allah, so call on Him by them" (7:180), and "Say: invoke Allah or invoke the Most Compassionate, by whatever name you invoke Him, to Him belong the Best Names" (17:110). Abū Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one. Whoever counts them will enter Paradise." This is in both Ṣaḥīḥs, and the names themselves are listed in a hadith recorded by at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah, with several differences between the two lists. In short, Allah is the name of the one Reality that holds in itself every attribute of perfection, the Creator and Sustainer, unique and without equal.

**"the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful"** translates ar-Raḥmān ar-Raḥīm. Both names come from the same root, raḥmah, mercy, and the pairing is a deliberate doubling: of all His names only these two are mentioned here, and both speak of mercy. Ar-Raḥmān carries more of the meaning of mercy than ar-Raḥīm, and Ibn Jarīr indicated that there is agreement on this. Al-Qurṭubī gave as the proof that the two names really are derived from "mercy" a hadith that at-Tirmidhī recorded and graded ṣaḥīḥ, in which ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf heard the Prophet ﷺ relate that Allah said, "I am ar-Raḥmān. I created the womb (raḥim) and gave it a name taken from My name. Whoever keeps it joined, I will keep him joined to Me, and whoever cuts it, I will cut him off." Al-Qurṭubī added that the Arabs rejected the name ar-Raḥmān only out of ignorance of Allah and His attributes.

What is the difference between the two? Several explanations were given. Abū ʿUbayd held that they mean the same thing, like the two Arabic words nadmān and nadīm for a companion. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said that ar-Raḥmān, which is Allah's alone, is the name that gathers up every kind of mercy He has, while ar-Raḥīm is the mercy that reaches the believers, as in the verse "He is ever Merciful (Raḥīm) to the believers" (33:43). Ibn ʿAbbās said they are two tender names, one of them more tender than the other. Al-ʿAzramī put it in a sentence that Ibn Jarīr recorded: "He is ar-Raḥmān with all creation and ar-Raḥīm with the believers." Those who explain it this way point out that when the Qur'an speaks of Allah rising over the Throne, the name it uses is ar-Raḥmān, "then He rose over the Throne, the Most Compassionate" (25:59) and "the Most Compassionate rose over the Throne" (20:5), to show that His mercy covers the whole of His creation, while it uses ar-Raḥīm for the believers in particular. So ar-Raḥmān is the broader name, the mercy that reaches all creatures in both worlds, and ar-Raḥīm is reserved for the believers. There is, all the same, a supplication that calls on Allah as "the Raḥmān and the Raḥīm of this world and the Hereafter". A simpler statement of the same idea is that ar-Raḥmān is the One whose mercy is shared by all, reaching the whole universe and whatever is still to be created, while ar-Raḥīm is the One whose mercy is perfect in every way a mercy can be. His mercy surrounds everything and embraces every living being, every blessing anyone has comes from it, and the believers receive the greatest share of it.

The two names also differ in who may carry them. Ar-Raḥmān is Allah's alone. "Say: invoke Allah or invoke ar-Raḥmān, by whatever name you invoke Him, to Him belong the Best Names" (17:110) puts the two names side by side as His, and "Ask those of Our Messengers whom We sent before you: did We ever appoint gods to be worshipped besides ar-Raḥmān?" (43:45) does the same. When Musaylimah the Liar styled himself the Raḥmān of Yamāmah, Allah exposed him and fixed the name "the Liar" to him so firmly that he is never mentioned without it, and he became a byword for lying among the settled people and the bedouin alike. Only he and those who followed his error ever called him by that name. It is not permissible to call any created being Raḥmān, since there cannot be anyone besides Allah whose mercy is all-embracing, and like the name "Allah" it has no dual and no plural. From this comes a practical ruling: those who shorten names like ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān or Faḍl ar-Raḥmān to plain "Raḥmān" are doing something that is not allowed and are committing a sin. Ar-Raḥīm, on the other hand, holds nothing that a creature cannot have, since one person can be perfectly merciful in dealing with another, and Allah Himself describes His Messenger ﷺ with it: "There has come to you a Messenger from among yourselves. It grieves him that you should suffer. He is anxious over you, and to the believers he is kind and merciful (raḥīm)" (9:128). He has done the same with other names of His, calling man "hearing and seeing" (76:2). So some of His names are shared with His creatures, and some, such as Allah, ar-Raḥmān, al-Khāliq the Creator and ar-Rāziq the Provider, belong to Him alone.

This explains the order of the three names. Allah began with the name that is exclusively His, then described it by ar-Raḥmān, which no one else may use and which is the softer and more general of the two names of mercy, and then by ar-Raḥīm. The most honoured names come first.

The fact that the only two attributes placed at the very opening of the Qur'an are both attributes of mercy carries a message of its own. It tells us that the heavens and the earth were created, and that the whole universe is kept in being, for no other reason than to display Allah's mercy. He had no need of any of it, and no one could compel Him to make it. It is His own mercy that called the whole order of things into existence and sustains it. The poet Rūmī put it in two lines of Persian whose sense is that there was nothing, neither our being nor any claim of ours to be, and it was Allah's mercy that heard what we had not yet said.

### Why does the Qur'an begin with a name?

Before Islam, in the Age of Ignorance, people opened whatever they did with the names of their idols and gods. The very first verse that Jibrīl (Gabriel) brought down to the Prophet ﷺ struck at that habit by commanding him to begin with the name of Allah: "Read with the name of your Lord." As-Suyūṭī said that the other revealed books also begin with "in the name of Allah". Other scholars held that the full formula, "in the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful", belongs to the Qur'an and to the community of Muhammad ﷺ alone. The two views agree with each other once it is said that all the revealed books share the trait of opening with Allah's name, while these exact words are peculiar to the Qur'an. Reports support this: the Prophet ﷺ used to open what he undertook with the words "bismika Allāhumma", "in Your name, O Allah", and when this verse was revealed he adopted its words instead, and from then on the practice was fixed by his command, his action or his approval. Al-Qurṭubī and Rūḥ al-Maʿānī both note this.

To begin a task in the name of Allah is to acknowledge that He is the Lord, the Being from whom every blessing comes and whose mercy pours continually over His creation, and to pray that He, in His infinite mercy, will come to one's help and bring the work to a good end. It is a person's admission that he is Allah's servant, and it carries with it the assurance of success.

Seen this way the basmalah gives the whole of a person's life a direction. The Qur'an and the hadiths repeat again and again that things are to be begun with Allah's name, and every time a Muslim does so he renews his side of the covenant with Allah: that nothing he does, not even his own existence, comes into being without Allah's will and help. That turns the ordinary business of living into worship. A disbeliever eats and drinks exactly as a Muslim does, but when the Muslim says bismillāh before he eats he is affirming that it was not in his power to obtain this one mouthful of food, which passed through countless stages between the sowing of a seed and the harvesting of the grain, and which needed the labour of the wind, the rain, the sun, the heavens and the earth and a thousand people, and that Allah alone brought it to him by carrying it through all of those stages. A disbeliever sleeps, wakes and goes about his day as a Muslim does, but the Muslim mentions Allah's name as he lies down and as he rises, and so renews his relationship with Him, and his worldly needs and errands take on the character of remembrance and are counted as acts of worship. When he says bismillāh as he climbs into a vehicle he is testifying that man had no power to produce it or to bring it to him, that only the order Allah created brought together from the corners of the world the wood, the steel and the other metals that went into it, the mechanics who shaped them and the driver, and placed this whole army of Allah's creatures at his service for the price of a few coins, coins which he did not create either, since Allah provided the elaborate means of earning them. An act that costs no time and no energy brings an immense return. The basmalah is the real philosopher's stone, one that turns not copper but mere dust into the purest gold, the profane into the sacred. Praise be to Allah for the religion of Islam and its teachings.

### Where is the basmalah said?

Saying bismillāh is recommended before starting any action. The Prophet ﷺ said that no important work receives Allah's blessing unless it is begun with His name. Another hadith extends it even to closing the door of one's house at night, putting out the lamp and covering a vessel. The Qur'an and the hadiths instruct that it be said when eating, when drinking, when performing wuḍūʾ, when mounting an animal or vehicle and when getting down from it, and al-Qurṭubī gathers these instructions together. Some of the particular occasions:

- Before a sermon.
- Before entering the place where one relieves oneself, about which there is a hadith.
- At the beginning of wuḍūʾ. Abū Hurayrah, Saʿīd ibn Zayd and Abū Saʿīd all related from the Prophet ﷺ, "There is no wuḍūʾ for the one who does not mention Allah's name over it," recorded by Aḥmad and the compilers of the Sunan, and it is a ḥasan hadith.
- Before eating. Muslim recorded that the Prophet ﷺ said to ʿUmar ibn Abī Salamah, then a boy in his care, "Say bismillāh, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is nearest to you." Some scholars held that the basmalah before eating is obligatory.
- Before marital relations. Ibn ʿAbbās reported, in a hadith in both Ṣaḥīḥs, that the Prophet ﷺ said that if a man says when he comes to his wife, "In the name of Allah. O Allah, keep Shayṭān away from us and keep Shayṭān away from what You grant us," and a child is decreed for them, Shayṭān will never be able to harm that child.

A hadith in the Musnad of Aḥmad shows what the name does. A man riding behind the Prophet ﷺ said that the animal stumbled and he said, "May Shayṭān perish." The Prophet ﷺ told him, "Do not say 'may Shayṭān perish', for when you say that he swells up and says, 'By my strength I threw him.' When you say bismillāh he shrinks until he is as small as a fly." An-Nasāʾī, in his book on the day and the night, and Ibn Mardawayh in his tafsīr record it from Usāmah ibn ʿUmayr, who said he was the one riding behind the Prophet ﷺ, and in that wording the Prophet ﷺ said that cursing Shayṭān makes him grow as big as a house, while saying bismillāh makes him as small as a fly. That is the blessing in the words.

Because the basmalah is a verse of the Qur'an, a part of a verse in Sūrat an-Naml and a full verse wherever it stands between two surahs, it is given the same respect as the rest of the Qur'an. It is not permissible to touch it without wuḍūʾ, and a person in a state of major ritual impurity, after intercourse, during menstruation or after childbirth, may not recite it as Qur'an until he or she has bathed. Such a person may, however, still say it as a prayer before beginning something, such as eating or drinking, in any condition.

### Is the basmalah a verse of this surah?

All Muslims agree that "In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful" is part of the Qur'an, since it occurs as part of a verse in Sūrat an-Naml, the twenty-seventh surah, in Sulaymān's (Solomon's) letter, and all agree that it is written at the head of every surah except Sūrat at-Tawbah, also called Barāʾah. What the scholars disagree about is whether it is a verse of al-Fātiḥah itself, a separate verse in front of every surah, or a verse of every surah it heads.

Three positions were held:

1. It is a verse of every surah except Barāʾah. This is attributed among the Companions to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn az-Zubayr, Abū Hurayrah and ʿAlī, among their Successors to ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Makḥūl and az-Zuhrī, and among the Imams it is the position of ash-Shāfiʿī, of Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh, of Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām, of ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Mubārak and, in one of the two reports from him, of Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal. Most of the reciters of Kūfah and a group of Companions and Successors counted it as the first of the seven verses of al-Fātiḥah. A hadith recorded by Ibn Khuzaymah supports this, and ad-Dāraquṭnī recorded a hadith from Abū Hurayrah that backs it up, and similar statements are attributed to ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās and others.
2. It is not a verse of al-Fātiḥah or of any other surah. This is the view of Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfah and their followers. In Abū Ḥanīfah's formulation it is a complete and independent verse of the Qur'an in its own right, revealed to be placed at the beginning of every surah to separate and mark off one surah from the next, and it is part of a surah only in an-Naml.
3. Dāwūd said that it is a separate verse at the beginning of every surah without being part of the surah itself, and this position too is attributed to Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal.

Umm Salamah's description of the Prophet's ﷺ recitation bears on the question. She said that he used to mark off each verse as he recited, slowly and distinctly, letter by letter: "In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful. All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds. The Most Compassionate, Most Merciful. Master of the Day of Judgment." Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Ḥibbān and al-Ḥākim recorded it, and ad-Dāraquṭnī graded its chain ṣaḥīḥ. A group of scholars recite the surah this way, pausing after the basmalah as a verse of its own, while others run the basmalah straight on into "All praise is for Allah".

### How is it used when reciting and praying?

One begins the recitation of the Qur'an with both sentences, "I seek refuge with Allah from Shayṭān, the accursed" and then "In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful", and during the recitation the basmalah is repeated, without the seeking of refuge, at the start of each new surah. The one exception is Barāʾah. When a reciter reaches it in the course of his reading he does not say the basmalah before it, but if he begins his recitation with that surah he says both the istiʿādhah and the basmalah. This is set out in the ʿĀlamgīrī from al-Muḥīṭ.

In the prayer:

- It is Sunnah to recite the basmalah after the istiʿādhah at the very beginning of the first rakʿah, and there is consensus that it is recited at the start of each following rakʿah as well. This is unanimously regarded as Sunnah, and some narrations describe reciting it at the start of every rakʿah as wājib, necessary.
- Whether it is said aloud or quietly is disputed. Abū Ḥanīfah and some other Imams prefer that it be said quietly. The whole question is set out in the next section.
- As for the surah that is read after al-Fātiḥah, the basmalah is not recited before it, whether the prayer is one recited aloud or one recited silently, because the practice is not reported from the Prophet ﷺ or from any of the first four caliphs. Sharḥ al-Munyah gives this as the view of Abū Ḥanīfah and Abū Yūsuf, and it is the view preferred in Sharḥ al-Munyah, ad-Durr al-Mukhtār, al-Burhān and other works. Imam Muḥammad, however, considered it preferable to recite the basmalah in that place when the prayer is a silent one, some reports attribute the same view to Abū Ḥanīfah himself, ash-Shāmī quoted a number of jurists in its favour, and it is the view adopted in Bahishti Zewar by Maulana Thanavi. Everyone agrees that reciting it in this position is not makrūh.

### Should the basmalah be recited aloud in prayer?

Those who do not count the basmalah as part of al-Fātiḥah naturally hold that it is not recited aloud. Those who do count it as a verse of every surah divided into two camps.

Ash-Shāfiʿī held that it is recited aloud together with al-Fātiḥah, and this was the opinion of many Companions, Successors and later Imams. Among the Companions it is the view of Abū Hurayrah, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās and Muʿāwiyah, and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr and al-Bayhaqī add ʿUmar and ʿAlī. Al-Khaṭīb reported it from all four caliphs, though the report from them is contradicted. A long list of Successors held it too. From the family of the Prophet ﷺ and the Companions: ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn and his son Muḥammad, ʿAlī ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās and his son Muḥammad, Sālim, and Nāfiʿ the freedman of Ibn ʿUmar. From the great teachers of tafsīr and law: Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, az-Zuhrī, Makḥūl, Ibn Sīrīn and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. And besides them Abū Wāʾil, Abū Qilābah, Abū ash-Shaʿthāʾ, Zayd ibn Aslam, Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit, al-Azraq ibn Qays, Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, ʿAbdullāh ibn Maʿqil ibn Muqarrin and Abū Bakr ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm. Al-Bayhaqī adds ʿAbdullāh ibn Ṣafwān and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah to the list, and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr adds ʿAmr ibn Dīnār.

Their reasoning is simple: if the basmalah is part of al-Fātiḥah, it is recited aloud like the rest of al-Fātiḥah. They also point to reports:

- Abū Hurayrah once led a prayer and recited the basmalah aloud, and when he had finished he said, "Of all of you, my prayer is the one most like the prayer of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." It is recorded in the Sunan of an-Nasāʾī, in the Ṣaḥīḥs of Ibn Khuzaymah and of Ibn Ḥibbān, and in al-Ḥākim's Mustadrak, and ad-Dāraquṭnī, al-Khaṭīb and al-Bayhaqī graded it ṣaḥīḥ.
- Anas ibn Mālik, asked about the Prophet's ﷺ recitation, said it was unhurried, and demonstrated by reciting "bismillāhi ar-Raḥmāni ar-Raḥīm" while drawing out the words. Al-Bukhārī recorded it.
- Umm Salamah's hadith above, in which the Prophet ﷺ recited the basmalah as a distinct verse at the head of the surah.
- Muʿāwiyah once led the prayer in Madinah and did not recite the basmalah, and the Muhājirūn who were present criticised him for it. When he led the next prayer he recited it aloud. Ash-Shāfiʿī and al-Ḥākim recorded this.

These reports are held to be sufficient proof for reciting it aloud. The counter-evidence, and the technical weighing of the narrations and their weaknesses, is a long discussion that need not be gone into here.

Others held that the basmalah is not recited aloud in the prayer. This was the established practice of the four caliphs and of ʿAbdullāh ibn Mughaffal, and the view of a number of the Successors and later scholars, and it is the position of Abū Ḥanīfah, ath-Thawrī and Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal. Mālik went further and held that it is not recited at all in the obligatory prayer, neither aloud nor quietly. This group relies on what Muslim recorded from ʿĀʾishah, that the Prophet ﷺ used to begin the prayer with the takbīr and then with "All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds", and on Anas ibn Mālik's statement in both Ṣaḥīḥs, "I prayed behind the Prophet ﷺ, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿUthmān, and they used to begin with 'All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds'," to which Muslim adds, "and they did not mention 'In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful' either at the beginning of the recitation or at its end." The Sunan collections record something similar from ʿAbdullāh ibn Mughaffal.

These are the views of the respected Imams, and for all their difference they agree on one thing: the prayer of the one who recites the basmalah aloud and the prayer of the one who recites it quietly are both valid. All favour is from Allah.

### Seeking refuge before the basmalah

Allah says, "So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge with Allah from Shayṭān, the accursed. Truly he has no power over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord. His power is only over those who take him as a friend and those who associate others with Allah" (16:98-100). Because of this verse the Muslims agree that it is Sunnah to say the taʿawwudh, "I seek refuge with Allah from Shayṭān, the accursed", before reciting the Qur'an, whether in the prayer or outside it, as Sharḥ al-Munyah states. The taʿawwudh belongs to recitation in particular. Other tasks are begun with the basmalah alone, and saying the taʿawwudh before them is not Sunnah, as the ʿĀlamgīrī notes in its chapter on disliked things.

"When you recite" means before you recite, in the same way that "when you intend to offer the prayer, wash your faces and your hands" (5:6) means before you stand to pray, as the hadiths show. The Prophet's ﷺ practice confirms it. Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said that when the Prophet ﷺ stood for the night prayer he would say the takbīr, then "All praise is Yours, O Allah, and all thanks. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You," then "There is no god but Allah" three times, and then, "I seek refuge with Allah, the Hearing, the Knowing, from Shayṭān the accursed, from his hamz, his nafkh and his nafth." Aḥmad recorded it, and so did the four compilers of the Sunan, and at-Tirmidhī called it the best known hadith on the subject. Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim related from his father that when the Prophet ﷺ began the prayer he would say three times "Allah is the Greatest, truly the Greatest," three times "All praise is for Allah, abundantly," three times "All praise is for Allah morning and evening," and then "O Allah, I seek refuge with You from Shayṭān the accursed, from his hamz, his nafkh and his nafth." Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah recorded it, and ʿAmr, one of its narrators, explained the three words: hamz is choking, nafkh is pride, and nafth is poetry. Ibn Mājah also recorded the same supplication from Ibn Masʿūd, with the explanation that hamz is death, nafkh is pride and nafth is poetry.

The same words are a remedy for anger. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said that two men were arguing in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ and one of them grew so angry that his nose swelled. The Prophet ﷺ said, "I know some words which, if he said them, would take away what he feels: 'I seek refuge with Allah from Shayṭān the accursed.'" Abū Yaʿlā recorded it in his Musnad, and an-Nasāʾī in his book on the day and the night. Sulaymān ibn Ṣurad told of a similar scene in al-Bukhārī's Ṣaḥīḥ: two men quarrelled in front of the Prophet ﷺ while the Companions sat with him, one began cursing the other with his face red with rage, and the Prophet ﷺ said, "I know a sentence which, if he said it, what he feels would leave him: 'I seek refuge with Allah from Shayṭān the accursed.'" The people told the man what the Prophet ﷺ had said, and he answered, "Am I mad?" Muslim, Abū Dāwūd and an-Nasāʾī also recorded it. There are many other hadiths on seeking refuge, which are gathered in the books of supplications and of the virtues of good deeds.

Why is this said before reading Allah's words and not before anything else? The istiʿādhah means: "I seek refuge with Allah from Shayṭān the accursed, so that he is kept from harming my religion or my worldly affairs, from holding me back from what I have been commanded, and from luring me into what I have been forbidden." Only Allah can keep Shayṭān's evil away from a human being. That is why Allah told us to be gentle and lenient with the human enemy, whose nature may soften under kindness until he turns from his wrong and even becomes a friend, but told us to seek refuge with Him from the devil, who accepts no bribe, is not touched by kindness, and wants nothing but the ruin of the children of Adam out of the hatred he has borne their father from the start. Only the One who created him can stop him. Three passages of the Qur'an, and only three, join these two commands together: "Show forgiveness, enjoin what is good and turn away from the ignorant. And if an evil whisper comes to you from Shayṭān, seek refuge with Allah. He is Hearing, Knowing" (7:199-200), where the first sentence is about dealing with people and the second about the devil. "Repel evil with what is better. We know best what they say. And say: My Lord, I seek refuge with You from the whisperings of the devils, and I seek refuge with You, my Lord, lest they come near me" (23:96-98). And "The good deed and the evil deed are not equal. Repel evil with what is better, and the one between whom and you there was enmity will become as though he were a close friend. None is granted this except those who are patient, and none is granted it except the owner of a great portion. And if an evil whisper from Shayṭān tries to turn you away, seek refuge with Allah. He is the Hearing, the Knowing" (41:34-36). The Qur'an is full of warnings about this enemy: "O children of Adam, do not let Shayṭān deceive you as he brought your parents out of Paradise" (7:27), "Shayṭān is an enemy to you, so treat him as an enemy. He only invites his followers so that they may be among the people of the Blaze" (35:6), and "Will you take him and his offspring as protectors instead of Me, when they are enemies to you? What an evil exchange for the wrongdoers" (18:50). He assured Adam that he was giving him sincere advice and was lying, so how will he deal with us after swearing, "By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, except Your chosen servants among them" (38:82-83)?

The istiʿādhah has its own virtues. It cleanses the mouth of the idle and foul talk it has been busy with and prepares it to recite the speech of Allah. It is a seeking of Allah's help and an acknowledgment that He is able to do all things. It is the servant's admission of his own weakness and helplessness before the enemy within, whom only Allah, who created him, can drive back and defeat. "Truly over My servants you have no authority, and your Lord is sufficient as a Guardian" (17:65). The contrast between the two enemies is sharp: a believer killed by the human enemy dies a martyr, while the one who falls to the inner enemy becomes a brigand, and a believer defeated by the outward enemy earns a reward, while one defeated by Shayṭān earns a sin and goes astray. Since Shayṭān sees a person from where the person cannot see him, it is fitting that the believer should take refuge from him with the One whom Shayṭān cannot see. Seeking refuge is a way of drawing near to Allah and a shelter with Him from the evil of every evil creature.

Is it required? The majority of scholars hold that the istiʿādhah, in the prayer and before reciting, is recommended rather than obligatory, so that leaving it out is not a sin. Ar-Rāzī recorded from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ that it is obligatory in the prayer and whenever one reads the Qur'an, and supported him with the apparent sense of the command "seek refuge", with the Prophet's ﷺ constant practice of it, and with the rule that whatever is needed to carry out a religious requirement is itself required, since warding off Shayṭān's evil is necessary. Saying "I seek refuge with Allah from Shayṭān the accursed" is enough to fulfil it.

### What do "Shayṭān" and "the accursed" mean?

The word Shayṭān comes from shaṭana, to be far away. The devil's nature is remote from that of mankind, and his wicked ways are far from every kind of goodness. Some said it comes instead from shāṭa, to burn, because he was created from fire, and some accepted both while preferring the first. Sībawayh settled it from usage: the Arabs say of a man that he has "tashayṭana" when he behaves like a devil, and if the word came from "burning" they would have said "tashayyaṭa". So the name means the far one, and it is given to every rebel among the jinn and among people. "So We appointed for every Prophet enemies, devils from among mankind and the jinn, inspiring one another with adorned speech as a delusion" (6:112). In Aḥmad's Musnad, Abū Dharr relates that the Prophet ﷺ said, "O Abū Dharr, seek refuge with Allah from the devils of mankind and of the jinn." Abū Dharr asked, "Are there human devils?" and he said, "Yes." In Muslim's Ṣaḥīḥ, Abū Dharr relates that the Prophet ﷺ said that a woman, a donkey or a black dog passing in front of a person who prays without a barrier interrupts the prayer, and when he asked what made the black dog different from a red or yellow one, the Prophet ﷺ said, "The black dog is a devil." Ibn Jarīr recorded with an authentic chain that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb once rode an animal that began to step proudly, and however much he struck it, it kept up its swagger, so he got down and said, "By Allah, you have carried me on a Shayṭān. I did not get off it until I felt something strange in my heart."

Ar-rajīm, "the accursed", means the one driven out, expelled from every kind of goodness, and the Qur'an uses the word of the devils pelted and driven from the heavens: "We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps and made them missiles to drive away the devils" (67:5), "We have adorned the nearest heaven with the stars, and as a guard against every rebellious devil. They cannot listen to the highest assembly, for they are pelted from every side, driven out, and theirs is a lasting torment, except the one who snatches a fragment, and then a piercing flame pursues him" (37:6-10), and "We have set the great stars in the heaven and beautified it for the beholders, and We have guarded it from every accursed devil, except the one who steals a hearing, and a clear flame pursues him" (15:16-18). There are several verses like these. It was also said that rajīm means the one who throws, because the devil throws doubts and evil thoughts into people's hearts, but the first meaning is the better known and the more accurate.

### What the letters say to the heart

Those who read the Qur'an for its allusions, in the taste of the people of recognition, found a message in the very letters of bi-smi. The bāʾ points to the splendour (bahāʾ) of Allah's Oneness, the sīn to the brilliance (sanāʾ) of the Self-Sufficient, and the mīm to the kingship (mulk) of His divinity: a splendour that stands by itself and is eternal and full of majesty, a brilliance that sustains itself and is generous and full of beauty, a kingship that lasts forever and knows no decline or annihilation. His splendour steals the heart, His brilliance increases love, and His majesty runs ahead of everything beautiful, so that in the language of the poets Venus rejoices to hear His music and the sun is jealous when it sees His beauty. Read another way, the bāʾ is His kindness (birr) to His servants, the sīn His secret (sirr) shared with His friends, and the mīm His favour (minnah) to those who yearn for Him. Without His kindness, how could the servant make himself ready for His secret? Without His favour, how could the servant reach union with Him or find a place at the threshold of His majesty? Without a love that had no beginning, how could the servant be at home with Him without end? How would water and clay ever have dared to love Him, had He not chosen them with His gentleness before time began? Love, the friends of Allah say, is His very Essence, and remembering His description drives away the sorrow of the sorrowful. This world is good only through His name, the next world only through His pardon, and the Garden only through the sight of Him. If it were not for His message and His name here, how could this world be a home for the servant? If it were not for His pardon and generosity there, the servant's case would be hard. And without the sight of Him in Paradise, the sight that lights up the heart, what would make a poor man happy? One of the masters of the Path prayed, "O Allah, we see by Your signs, we live in knowing You, we flourish by Your name, we are happy in remembering You, and we rejoice in finding You." He went on that it is they who are drunk with love from His cup and they who are caught in His snare, and the lovers' verses say that since the sermon of His love was read in the servant's name, the whole world seems to follow the servant's heart.

It has been said that ism, name, comes from simah, a brand or mark. Whoever says "in the name of Allah" receives that stamp and is marked with that brand, and the one who wears the king's brand is safe from the police by day and the patrols by night. Whoever finds a name finds it at His threshold, so be one of His and stop worrying about anyone else. ʿAlī ibn Mūsā ar-Riḍā said, "When the servant says 'in the name of Allah', its meaning is: I have branded myself with the brand of my Lord." On which the lover adds: O Lord, I wear Your brand and am happy in it, but I grieve over my own existence. O Generous One, take my being out of my way, so that Your being may set all my affairs right. The master of the Path said, "O Allah, when Your light lit the lamp of recognition, my heart grew. When Your testimony became my spokesman, my voice grew. When Your nearness lit the lamp of ecstasy, my aspiration grew. When Your desire put my work in order, my effort grew. When Your being set my affairs right, my being grew. O Allah, what have I ever seen from my own being but trial and trouble, while from Your being everything is gift and loyalty? O You who are manifest in kindness and plain in generosity, count what I have done as not done, and do what is fitting for You."

Someone may ask: the Book and the Sunnah contain many names of Allah, all of them great, eternal, pure and beautiful, so what is the wisdom in opening the mighty Qur'an with these three and no others? One answer given is that He chose these three and stopped at them so that His servants would find it easy to call on Him by His names without any loss of reward, since He knew they could never hold so many names in their memory.

### In short

- The basmalah means "with the name of Allah, with His help and with His blessing, I begin." Its three names are placed in order of honour: Allah, the name of His Essence that belongs to Him alone, then ar-Raḥmān, the all-embracing mercy that no creature may be called by, then ar-Raḥīm, the mercy that reaches the believers and that a merciful person can share.
- Islam put Allah's name where the pagans had put the names of their gods. Said before eating, drinking, travelling, wuḍūʾ, intimacy and every important act, it turns daily life into worship and shrinks Shayṭān to the size of a fly.
- It is agreed to be part of the Qur'an and written before every surah except at-Tawbah. Whether it is a verse of al-Fātiḥah was disputed: ash-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad in one report and many Companions and Successors said yes, Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfah said it is a separate verse of division. Whether to say it aloud in prayer was disputed in the same way, and the prayer is valid either way.
- Before reciting the Qur'an one first says "I seek refuge with Allah from Shayṭān, the accursed," a Sunnah by consensus that most scholars hold is recommended rather than obligatory. It clears the mouth for Allah's words, confesses one's weakness before an enemy who accepts no kindness, and is also the cure for anger.
- Shayṭān means "the far one", far from every good, and rajīm means the one driven out. The two names of mercy at the head of the Qur'an announce that mercy, not need, is the reason the universe exists.

2.text:
The surah opens with the words "All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds". It is the first thing a Muslim says in every unit of prayer, and it is the first of three verses of praise before the surah turns, in its last three verses, into a request. This verse is a statement, not a request. It is also a lesson. Allah praises Himself here, and in doing so He teaches His servants how to praise Him, as if He had said, "Say: all praise is for Allah."

The verse makes two claims. First, that every kind of praise belongs to Allah, for who He is and for what He does. Second, that He is the Lord, the owner and nurturer, of every world there is. The second claim is the proof of the first. If He alone sustains everything that exists, then He alone deserves the praise that anything in existence can earn.

### Phrase by phrase

**"All praise"** translates al-ḥamd. Ḥamd is praise for someone's qualities as well as for their deeds, which makes it wider than thanks, since thanks is only for something done. The "al" in front of it (the Arabic "the") gathers up every kind of praise and thanks there is and gives all of it to Allah. A supplication of the Prophet ﷺ makes the same point:

> "O Allah, all praise is Yours, all dominion is Yours, all good is in Your hand, and to You all matters return."

**"is for Allah"** means it belongs to Him purely and alone, not to any of the things people worship instead of Him and not to any creature. Ibn Jarīr explained that it is His for favours too many to count. He gave people the bodies and faculties with which they are able to obey Him. He gives them their provision in this life and a comfortable living, though nothing obliges Him to. And He warned them and showed them the way to earn a home of everlasting happiness. From first to last, all of it is His.

**"Lord"** translates Rabb. A rabb is an owner with full authority over what he owns, a master, the one with the right to lead. In its root sense the word means the one who nurtures: who brings a thing along by gradual stages, in the way that is good for it, until it is complete. On its own, Rabb is used only for Allah. For anyone else it has to be qualified, as in rabb ad-dār, the master of the house, because a created being needs nurture itself and cannot truly nurture anything. It is also reported that ar-Rabb is Allah's greatest name.

**"of all worlds"** translates al-ʿālamīn, the plural of ʿālam. An ʿālam is everything in existence other than Allah, and the word is itself a plural with no singular, so "worlds" is a plural of a plural. Every kind of creation, in the heavens and the earth, on land and at sea, is a world of its own, and so is every generation. The word comes from ʿalāmah, a sign, because every created thing is a sign that points to its Creator and to His oneness.

### Why praise belongs to Allah alone

Whoever praises anything, anywhere, is in reality praising Allah. The world is full of things that draw admiration for their beauty or usefulness, but behind each of them is the same creative power. Admiring a work of craft is admiration of the craftsman. This short sentence pulls a person out of the maze of many things and shows how they are all knit into one. Only ignorance or inattention makes anyone give the praise to someone else.

That has a consequence. If one Being alone deserves all praise, then that Being alone deserves worship. So although the phrase is worded as praise, it cuts the root of worshipping created things and states, as something self-evident, the first principle of the faith: the oneness of Allah. Praise is His for His essence, His attributes and His actions. He created everything, everything belongs to Him, and He manages all of it. He gives blessings to individuals in particular and to humankind in general.

Ibn ʿAbbās put the reasons simply: praise is Allah's because He is kind to His creatures, so they praise Him. It was also said that it is His because of His endless blessings on the servants He guided to believe in Him. And it was also said that praise, pure oneness and divinity all belong to Allah, who has no child, no partner, no helper and no assistant.

### A statement Allah loves

ʿUmar once said to ʿAlī: we know "there is no god but Allah", "glory be to Allah" and "Allah is greatest", but what about "all praise is for Allah"? ʿAlī answered that it is a statement Allah liked for Himself, was pleased with for Himself, and loves to hear repeated. Ibn ʿAbbās called it the statement of gratitude, and said that when a servant says al-ḥamdu lillāh, Allah says, "My servant has praised Me." Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded this.

The Prophet ﷺ said the same in many ways. When al-Aswad ibn Sarīʿ offered to recite to him some words of praise he had composed for his Lord, the Prophet ﷺ told him, "Your Lord loves praise." Aḥmad and an-Nasāʾī recorded it. Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh reported him saying that the best remembrance of Allah is "there is no god but Allah" and the best supplication is "all praise is for Allah". At-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah recorded it, and at-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan gharīb (sound, with a rare chain). Anas ibn Mālik reported, in a hadith recorded by Ibn Mājah, that whenever Allah gives a servant a blessing and the servant says "all praise is for Allah", what he has given back is better than what he received.

Ibn ʿUmar reported, in another hadith recorded by Ibn Mājah, that a servant once said, "My Lord, Yours is the praise that befits the majesty of Your face and the greatness of Your authority." The two recording angels did not know how to write it down. They went up and told Allah that a servant had said something they could not record. Allah knew exactly what he had said, but He asked them what it was. When they repeated it, He said, "Write it as My servant said it, until he meets Me and I reward him for it."

### What Allah says back when you say it

Abū Hurayrah reported, in a hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah said: "The prayer is divided between Me and My servant, and My servant will have what he asks for." When the servant says "All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds," Allah says, "My servant has paid Me homage." The dialogue continues through the rest of the surah: the next verse is answered with "My servant has praised Me", the one after with "My servant has proclaimed My greatness", the fifth verse is shared between Allah and His servant, and the request for guidance is answered with "This is for My servant, and My servant will have what he asked for."

### How many worlds are there?

Scholars drew the boundary of "the worlds" in different places. Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayd said it covers everything with a mind, meaning jinn, humans, angels and devils, but not animals. Zayd ibn Aslam and Abū Muḥaysin said it covers everything Allah created with a soul. Qatādah said every kind of creation is a world. Az-Zajjāj said it covers everything Allah created in this life and the next, and al-Qurṭubī held that this is the correct view. The Qur'an itself supports it: when Pharaoh asked, "And what is the Lord of all worlds?", Mūsā (Moses) answered, "The Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything between them, if you would only be sure" (26:23-24).

On this reading the worlds include the sky, the earth, the sun, the moon, the stars, wind and rain, angels, jinn, animals, plants, minerals and people, and whatever other universes may lie beyond ours. Imam ar-Rāzī argued that reason can show there is unlimited space beyond our universe, and that Allah, who is able to do all things, could have created millions of other universes in it. It is reported from the Companion Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that there are forty thousand worlds, and ours, from east to west, is only one of them. Muqātil put the number at eighty thousand. To the objection that nothing could live in outer space without our kind of air, ar-Rāzī replied that beings elsewhere need not be built the way we are, and may be made of different stuff with different needs. He suggested this some eight hundred years before anyone travelled into space, and the guesses of modern science point the same way.

Ibn ʿAbbās explained "Lord of all worlds" as Lord of everything with a spirit that walks the earth and of everyone who lives in heaven. It was also said to mean the Master of the jinn and of humankind. And it was also said to mean the One who created everything that exists, provides for all of it, and moves it from one state to the next.

### What the order of the universe is telling you

Seen through this phrase, the universe is an immensely complex but perfectly joined order. From the heavens down to a speck of dust, everything is linked in one chain and doing the task assigned to it. A single mouthful of food reaches a person only because a thousand forces of sky and earth have worked together to produce it. That order is there to be thought about. If Allah has put millions of His creatures to work for human beings, then human beings cannot be pointless. The Qur'an insists that the universe is not absurd: "We have not created the heavens and the earth and everything between them in vain. That is the assumption of the disbelievers" (38:27). And it names the purpose of the one the universe serves: "I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me" (51:56).

This is also why praise comes first in the surah. The whole opening chapter puts into words the feelings that rise in a person who has found the truth. Anyone who looks at the world sees Allah's power and mercy everywhere, an astonishing order and care, everything fitted to human needs. Praise is the natural response. The same observation then leads to the rest of the surah. A machine this great cannot run for nothing. So there must be a day when the grateful and the ungrateful are repaid, and the request for guidance follows from that. The surah is a miniature of the faith, and the rest of the Qur'an enlarges the picture.

### Praise at seeing blessings and praise at seeing the Giver

There is also an inner reading of the verse. It is praise of the lovingly kind God, the Creator who provides. He is found without being sought, known without being grasped, and loved without being seen. He is powerful without effort and self-subsisting without change. His kingship never declines. He has no beginning and no end, and He is described by majesty and by beauty. He saw that His servants could never measure Him, as the Qur'an says: "They have not given Allah His due measure" (6:91). So in His generosity He appointed them His deputies in praising Him, taught them how, and gave them permission. Otherwise who would have dared to say "praise belongs to Allah" if He had not said it first?

On this reading praise is of two kinds. One comes from seeing blessings: it extols Him, puts His gifts to work in obedience, and gives thanks so that blessings increase today and lead to Paradise tomorrow. The Prophet ﷺ said that the first people called to the Garden will be those who praise Allah fully in every state. The other kind comes from seeing the Giver Himself, when the one who praises forgets everything else, including himself: he hears One, sees One and reaches One. As one of the early masters of the path said, the two worlds became lost in love, love became lost in the Beloved, and he could no longer say whether it was he or He.

"Lord of all worlds" is read in the same spirit as the Nurturer of everyone in the world, who assigns each one a portion. For one person the portion is nourishment of the body with blessings, for another nourishment of the heart with the Giver of blessings. Blessings go to those who keep working in His service, the secret of the Giver to those whose only hope is to see Him. The Prophet ﷺ pointed to that second nourishment when he said, "I spend the night with my Lord, and He feeds me and gives me drink." He did not eat fine food or drink fine drinks, and he warned others against indulging in blessings. When they asked him why he did not eat, he said he was already drunk on the wine of being together with his Lord. It is said that this drink was special to him alone, the one who was shown the greatest signs and whose eye "did not wander, nor did it overreach" (53:17). He said he had a moment with Allah that no angel brought near and no prophet sent could share, and even the prophets, all one hundred and twenty-four thousand of them, came hoping for a taste of it. Allah nurtures the souls of worshippers with confirmation, the hearts of the pure with greater strength, and the states of those who truly know Him with tawḥīd, the pure oneness of Allah. Someone nurtured on that has little use for ordinary food. When a snake bites someone, you give him the antidote, not sweets. A story about Yazīd Hārūn makes the point. He forbade his student ʿUtbah al-Ghulām to eat dates, yet ate them himself. When the student's mother objected, he said, "Your son wants dates, but dates want me. They are allowed for me and not for him." The people of the world want food, but food wants people like these. It is in that sense that the report says Paradise longs for Salmān.

### In short

- "All praise" means every kind of praise and thanks, and all of it belongs to Allah alone, for who He is and for what He gives.
- Because He alone deserves all praise, He alone deserves worship: the verse states the oneness of Allah as something self-evident.
- "Lord" means the owner and nurturer who brings everything to completion by stages, and the word belongs to Allah alone.
- "All worlds" is every kind of creation, in this life and the next, and the ordered universe they form is itself the proof that praise is His.
- Saying al-ḥamdu lillāh is a statement Allah loves, the best of supplications, and one He answers with "My servant has praised Me."

3.text:
After naming Allah as Lord of all worlds, the surah describes Him with the words "the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful". These are the same two names that stood in the basmalah, ar-Raḥmān and ar-Raḥīm, and their meaning is explained there. What matters here is their placement. Allah has just been called the Lord who owns and governs everything that exists, a title with weight and warning in it, and before the surah goes on to the Day of Judgment it pauses to say that this Lord is merciful, twice over.

### Phrase by phrase

**"the Most Compassionate"** is ar-Raḥmān, and **"Most Merciful"** is ar-Raḥīm. Both come from raḥmah, mercy, and both are intensive forms, the kind of Arabic word that expresses a quality in its highest degree. The first speaks of the sheer abundance of Allah's mercy, the second of its perfection. Together they say that His mercy covers His creation, and that the believers are the ones who receive the greatest share of it. Mercy, in the sense the word carries here, is to want good for those who deserve it, and both names describe Him as gentle.

### Why mercy follows "Lord of all worlds"

Al-Qurṭubī pointed out that Allah describes Himself as the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful immediately after calling Himself Lord of all worlds, so that the verse holds a warning followed by an encouragement. The Qur'an pairs the two in the same way elsewhere: "Tell My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful, and that My punishment is the painful punishment" (15:49-50), and "Your Lord is swift in punishment, and He is Forgiving, Merciful" (6:165). "Lord" makes a person fear, and "the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful" makes him hope. A hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim shows how large both sides are: the Prophet ﷺ said that if the believer knew what punishment Allah has, no one would hope for His Paradise, and if the disbeliever knew what mercy Allah has, no one would despair of it.

There is a second reason for naming mercy at this point. The previous verse said that Allah is the Lord, the One who brings up and sustains all worlds. Naming His mercy straight afterwards is a reminder that He did not take on the nurturing of His whole creation under any outside compulsion or inner need or necessity of any kind, but in answer to the demand of His own quality of mercy. If this universe did not exist, He would lose nothing by its absence, and now that it does exist, it is no burden to Him.

### Two mercies, two kinds of servant

Read for its inner meaning, the pairing of the names describes two ways Allah deals with people. He is the Most Compassionate in that He gives life, and the Most Merciful in that He shows Himself: the first is done through acts of kindness, the second through lights. As the Most Compassionate He smooths the road of the wage-earner, the servant who toils in hope of the maidens and palaces of Paradise. As the Most Merciful He lights the candle of friendship on the road of His friends, who are flooded with light in the sea of seeing Him face to face, and who say that on the day they reach union with Him they will think nothing of the state of the people of Paradise. He gives the strivers success in their struggle and gives the finders the realisation of contemplation. The first is the state of the one who desires, the second the state of the one who is desired. The desirer sets out with the lamp of success and reaches contemplation, the desired sets out with the candle of realisation and reaches vision. Contemplation is what happens when the barriers between the servant and the Real are lifted. Vision is a seeing in which the servant is not absent for a moment: he looks on love with the eye of response, on the Present with the eye of presence, on the Solitary with the eye of solitude. By distance from himself he draws near to Allah's nearness, by losing himself he grows familiar with His manifestness, by absence from himself he becomes present before His generous presence. For Allah is not far from the strivers, not lost to the seekers, and not absent from those who desire Him. A prayer in this spirit asks Him to have mercy on the hearts of His creatures and come out from behind the veil, so that the seventy-two sects can end their quarrels.

### In short

- The two names of the basmalah return, now right after "Lord of all worlds": warning first, then encouragement, fear then hope.
- Allah's punishment is such that a believer who saw it would despair, and His mercy such that a disbeliever who saw it would hope. Both are real.
- Allah sustains the universe out of mercy, not need. Its existence costs Him nothing and its absence would take nothing from Him.
- The Most Compassionate eases the road of the one who works for reward, and the Most Merciful lights the road of the one who seeks Him for His own sake.

4.text:
The third description of Allah in the surah is "Master of the Day of Judgment". The previous two verses looked at the whole of creation, the "all worlds" that He brings up and the mercy He pours over them. This verse looks forward to a single day, the day on which every creature will be brought back to life, called to account and repaid for what it did, and it says that the mastery of that day is His. It is the verse that gives the surah its seriousness. Praise and mercy come first, but the one who prays is reminded, before he makes any request, that he is heading towards a reckoning and that the only authority on that day will be the One he is addressing.

Read in the natural order of human thought, the verse is where a person's reflection arrives on its own. Whoever looks at the world around him cannot miss the power and the mercy that are evident everywhere, and the extraordinary order and supervision in everything he sees, all of it fitted to human needs. A machine so vast and so exact cannot be in vain, and so there has to come a day when the grateful and the ungrateful are repaid for how they lived. The prayer that rises from that realisation is: Lord, You are the Master of the Day of Judgment.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Master"** translates mālik. The word comes from milk, ownership, which means possessing a thing in such a way that one has the right and the power to dispose of it as one likes, and this is the sense given in the Qāmūs. The verse does not say what is owned, and according to al-Kashshāf this silence is the point: the phrase covers everything without exception, so that on the Day of Judgment the ownership of all that exists belongs to Allah alone. The word has been read in two ways. Read as malik, it means the King, and says that His kingship alone will be visible on that day. Read as mālik, the Owner, it says that He holds the whole affair of the Day of Resurrection in His hand. In either reading the word can stand as an adjective of the definite noun before it, because He is described by it at all times, in the same way that He is called "Forgiver of sin".

**"of the Day of"** is yawm, and the verse ties His ownership to one day in particular, for reasons explained below. Another rendering of the whole phrase is the Arbitrator of the Day of Judgment, the day of reckoning and of the settling of every dispute between created beings, when people are judged by their deeds and there is no judge but Him.

**"Judgment"** translates ad-dīn, which here means recompense, requital, the settling of accounts, with reward or punishment. The Qur'an uses the word in that sense when it says "On that Day Allah will pay them their just due (dīnahum) in full" (24:25), and when the people of Paradise recall their doubt, "Shall we really be judged (madīnūn)?" (37:53). Ibn ʿAbbās said that the Day of Dīn is the day of recompense for all creatures, meaning the Day of Judgment, when Allah will call His creation to account for their deeds, evil for evil and good for good, except those He pardons. Many other Companions, Successors and scholars of the Salaf said the same, because this is the plain and obvious meaning of the verse.

### Why single out that day?

Allah's ownership of the Day of Judgment does not cancel His ownership of everything else. He has just been called Lord of all worlds, which includes this life and the next. The day is named because on that day no one but Him will be able to claim ownership of anything at all, and no one will even speak without His permission: "On the Day when the Spirit (ar-Rūḥ, Jibrīl or another angel) and the angels stand in rows, they will not speak except the one the Most Compassionate permits, and he will say what is right" (78:38), "All voices will be hushed before the Most Compassionate, and you will hear nothing but a faint shuffle of feet" (20:108), and "When that Day comes, no soul will speak except by His leave. Some of them will be wretched and some blessed" (11:105). Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk related that Ibn ʿAbbās explained the verse in a sentence: on that day no one owns anything of what they used to own in the world.

The fuller answer takes two steps. First, who is the real master? A moment's reflection shows that the true owner of every particle of dust in the universe can only be the One who created it and brings it up, whose mastery is complete, without beginning or end, covering the living and the dead, the visible and the hidden, the seen and the unseen. Man's mastery, by contrast, is fenced in by a "before", when it did not exist, and an "after", when it will exist no longer. It reaches the living and not the dead, the seen and not the unseen, the outside of things and not their inside. So the real Master of the whole universe, in this world as much as on the Day of Judgment, is none but Allah. Second, why then specify that day? Because Allah, in His generosity and wisdom, has given man a kind of imperfect, temporary and outward mastery too, and the Sharīʿah, in regulating worldly affairs, takes man's limited right of ownership into account. But man, holding land, money or power that was given to him as a trial, is always liable to become drunk with pride and conceit. "Master of the Day of Judgment" is the warning to a man reeling in forgetfulness and self-importance that all his possessions and all his relationships with things and people are short-lived, and that a day is coming when masters will no longer be masters and slaves no longer slaves, when nobody will hold even the appearance of owning anything, and when the ownership of the whole universe, outward as well as real, will be seen to belong to Allah and to no one else. Sūrat al-Muʾmin, also called Ghāfir, the fortieth surah, serves as a commentary on this phrase. On that day Allah will ask, "To whom belongs the kingdom today?" and no one, however high his station, will answer, so He will answer Himself: "To Allah, the One, the Overpowering" (40:16). "On the Day they come forth, nothing of theirs is hidden from Allah. Today every soul is recompensed for what it earned. No wrong is done today. Allah is swift in reckoning" (40:17).

### Allah is the true King

The hadiths press the same point. Allah is the true Owner, "the King, the Holy, the One free from every defect" (59:23). Abū Hurayrah reported, in a hadith in both Ṣaḥīḥs, that the Prophet ﷺ said that the most despicable name in Allah's sight is a man who calls himself the king of kings, when there is no owner but Allah. Both Ṣaḥīḥs also record that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah will seize the earth and fold up the heavens in His Right Hand and proclaim, "I am the King. Where are the kings of the earth? Where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogant?" When the Qur'an calls a human being a king, it is a figure of speech, as when it says "Allah has appointed Ṭālūt (Saul) as king over you" (2:247), "there was a king behind them" (18:79) and, of the Children of Israel, "He made prophets among you and made you kings" (5:20), and as when the Prophet ﷺ described some of his community sailing to war "like kings on their thrones", in a hadith in both Ṣaḥīḥs.

The inner reading says the same thing in its own words. The verse points to the permanence of the kingship of the One and the unending compelling power of the Godhead. Every king's empire has its day, then it ends and vanishes, his kingship finishes and his state changes. Allah's kingship is permanent, today and tomorrow, and never comes to an end. In both worlds nothing and no one lies outside His kingship and rule, and no one has a kingship like His. He is Lord of the worlds today and will be Owner of the Day of Judgment tomorrow, which no creature can say of itself. Where, then, is the servant's power to act? Ownership and kingship in both worlds are Allah's, without partner, condition or need, and "your Lord creates what He wills and chooses. They have no choice" (28:68). The one who owns nothing rules nothing.

### Taking account of yourself before you are taken to account

Since dīn is reckoning, the verse is a call to begin the reckoning now. A hadith says that the wise person is the one who calls himself to account and works for what comes after death. ʿUmar said: "Call yourselves to account before you are called to account, weigh yourselves before you are weighed, and prepare for the great presentation before the One from whom nothing of your deeds is hidden," and he recited "That Day you will be presented, and no secret of yours will stay hidden" (69:18).

A gentler side of the reckoning is also noticed. Since Allah says, in effect, that He alone owns and takes charge of calling His servants to account, no one else will learn of their faults, and so no one will be shamed before others. The reckoning itself is a severity, but to keep the veil in place while it is done is pure generosity, and that is His way: whenever He strikes a blow of severity, He lays on it the balm of generosity. One of the masters of the Path said that if, tomorrow at the place of reckoning, he has anything to offer and is given leave to speak, he will say, "Lord God, of three things that I have, look at one: a prostration that never wanted anything from You but a heart, an assent by which I called true whatever You said, and a spirit and a heart that have wanted nothing but You since the wind of generosity first rose."

### Why the Day of Judgment is real, and reasonable

Two questions arise once the words are clear: what is this Day, and why does it exist? The Day of Judgment is the day Allah has appointed for repaying good and evil deeds. This world is the field of action, the place where a person is required to do his duty, not the place where he is paid. A man's being healthy, rich or powerful does not prove that he has won Allah's favour, and a man's being ill, poor, weak or miserable does not prove that he is under His anger. Even in worldly terms this is obvious: a man sweating in a factory or an office does not count his sweat a misfortune. Take his chance to sweat away from him and you have earned his deepest displeasure, because beyond the toil he can see the wages coming at the end of the month. The same principle explains why the greatest sufferings in this world fall to the prophets and, after them, to the people of Allah, who are nonetheless content and even happy. Physical well-being, worldly glory and comfort are no sure sign of virtue and truthfulness, and sorrow and suffering are no sure sign of wrongdoing and falsehood. It can happen that a person receives some punishment or reward for his deeds in this world, but it is never the full repayment, only a faint sample shown as a hint or a warning: "We will surely make them taste the nearer punishment before the greater punishment, so that they may return" (32:21), and "Such is the punishment, and the punishment of the Hereafter is far greater, if only they knew" (68:33). What this world brings, whether suffering or joy, is sometimes a test and sometimes a punishment, but it is never the full repayment, because the world itself is passing. What really counts is the joy or suffering that lasts forever, which a person will come to know in the world beyond this one.

Put the two facts together, that deeds are not fully repaid here, and that justice and reason both demand that good and evil, being unequal, should each be repaid according to its kind, and it follows that beyond this world there must be another in which every deed, large or small, good or evil, is judged and justly rewarded or punished. The Qur'an calls that world al-Ākhirah, the Hereafter, and its day al-Qiyāmah, the Resurrection, or Yawm ad-Dīn, the Day of Recompense. The Qur'an itself lays out the argument: "The blind and the seeing are not equal, nor are those who believe and do good and the wrongdoer. How little you reflect. The Hour is surely coming, there is no doubt about it, yet most people do not believe" (40:58-59).

### In short

- Mālik means the owner with full right to dispose of what he owns, and ad-dīn means recompense. On the Day of Judgment every creature is raised, called to account and repaid, and ownership of everything belongs openly to Allah alone.
- Allah owns everything now too. The day is singled out because on it no one will own anything, no one will speak without His leave, and the pride that possessions breed in man will be seen for what it was.
- "King of kings" is the most hateful title in Allah's sight. Human kingship is a figure of speech, and "Whose is the kingdom today? Allah's, the One, the Overpowering" is the last word on it.
- This world is the field of work, not the payroll. Health and wealth prove nothing, suffering proves nothing, and justice itself requires a day when every deed is fully repaid.
- Call yourself to account before you are called, and know that the One who takes the account keeps the veil over His servants' faults.

5.text:
